current_answer: Treat stale serving as a four-gate decision: the response must be storable at the named cache, its effective freshness lifetime must have elapsed, a bounded stale permission must apply, and no stronger revalidation rule may block stale reuse. Private caches normally use max-age; shared caches use s-maxage before max-age and Expires. stale-while-revalidate may return old bytes while a supporting cache validates, and stale-if-error may return them for a defined error, but neither extension grants storage, fixes a cache key, clears a browser or service worker, or guarantees implementation support. Under the portable RFC 9111 reading, do not treat either extension as an override for no-cache, must-revalidate, proxy-revalidate, or shared s-maxage revalidation semantics. Use ETag or Last-Modified for the ordinary validation path; If-None-Match wins when both conditions are present. Diagnose old content with named Cache-Status, Age, Via, provider fields, validators, and a correlated origin marker, while treating missing or single-hop evidence as unknown. This 25 Sep 2026 follow-up is documentation-only: no live stale response, 304, provider, browser, origin, purge, or invalidation result is claimed. A service-worker update also does not replace an open document or automatically clear script-managed Cache Storage: a candidate must be checked, installed, and activated; it normally waits for old clients, while skipWaiting can change their controller without reloading page code. Keep old fingerprinted assets and worker-cache entries through the supported compatibility window, then retire them under an explicit app policy. This 28 Sep 2026 follow-up is documentation-only; no browser, worker, origin, or deployment behavior was tested. For redirects, inspect the response to each requested URI: each hop has its own status, Location, key, and freshness. A stored redirect may retain an old Location; a current first hop does not prove later hops are current. Use explicit freshness or validation when a bounded route-change window matters. A new no-store response does not erase an older redirect. The final URL alone does not identify the hop or cache that supplied it. Browser HTTP-cache partitioning adds a user-agent context dimension: the Fetch Standard uses a network partition key with top-level site as its first component and leaves a second component null or implementation-defined. It does not replace RFC 9111 method/target-URI matching, Vary, storage, freshness, or validation, and it does not configure a CDN or proxy. Use private/no-store response policy for the intended storage audience; partitioning is not a privacy guarantee. Chrome/Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit describe implementation-specific details and exceptions. The A/B context examples in the 4 Oct 2026 follow-up are expected, not tested; no browser or cache was measured.

catalogue_card.question: How can web developers choose correct HTTP cache headers and diagnose stale content without accidentally caching private responses?
catalogue_card.text: When old bytes appear, separate storage permission, browser/private max-age, shared s-maxage, bounded stale permission, and conditional validation. Use named-hop evidence to distinguish an expected stale/revalidation path from an unexplained copy, and keep private/sensitive responses out of shared storage. For service-worker deploys, distinguish worker activation from page reload and application-directed Cache Storage cleanup. For a moved URL that still lands at an old destination, record each redirect response and Location separately; do not infer the supplying cache from the final URL or Age alone. Browser partitioning can add a top-level-site dimension to browser-local HTTP-cache selection, but it does not replace HTTP policy or configure a shared intermediary; the cited context comparison is expected, not tested.

summary: The checks common to CloudFront and Cloudflare are representation review, storage audience, explicit browser/shared freshness, validators, key review, named-hop evidence, and downstream limits.
Use no-store when intentional HTTP-cache retention is unacceptable; use private, no-cache when browser retention with validation is acceptable and shared storage is not allowed.
For safely public mutable content, set max-age and s-maxage deliberately and use validators; s-maxage controls shared-cache freshness separately from browser max-age.
For immutable changed bytes, prefer a new versioned or content-hash URL; a new URL is not deletion of the old URL.
If-None-Match is evaluated before If-Modified-Since when both conditions are present; a 304 does not identify the serving hop.
The minimum HTTP cache-key model is method plus target URI, with Vary and deployment-specific key inputs layered on top; TTL cannot repair a key collision.
In an incident, first ask whether a network request occurred, then inspect named-hop fields and correlate a redacted origin marker with a counter.
Age, Cache-Status, Via, CF-Cache-Status, and CloudFront Server-Timing metrics are scoped evidence with different standards or vendor boundaries; missing fields are unknown.
CloudFront positive minimum TTL and response-header policies are CloudFront-specific; a viewer Cache-Control value is not proof of edge TTL.
Cloudflare Origin Cache Control, matching Cache Rule, Edge/Browser TTL, custom key, and purge scope are separate Cloudflare controls; keep them separate from CloudFront and HTTP rules.
A named-provider purge or invalidation is not universal eviction: browser, service-worker, corporate-proxy, history, other edge, and application copies remain downstream limits.
This run is documentation-only/no live provider capture; no deployment, incident, privacy, freshness, purge, invalidation, or browser result is claimed.
A stale response needs four gates: allowed storage, an elapsed effective lifetime, an applicable stale permission, and no stronger prohibition blocking reuse.
Private caches normally apply max-age; shared caches apply s-maxage before max-age and Expires. The same object can be fresh in one cache and stale in another.
stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error are bounded, support-dependent permissions; they do not grant storage, shared safety, key correctness, purge, or browser/service-worker eviction.
Under the portable RFC 9111 reading, do not treat stale extensions as overrides for no-cache, must-revalidate, proxy-revalidate, or shared s-maxage revalidation semantics.
A 304 permits reuse of stored bytes at the evaluating recipient; it does not identify the hop, prove origin contact, or prove application freshness.
Cache-Status fwd=stale, fwd-status, hit, ttl, Age, Via, provider fields, and origin markers are scoped evidence. Missing fields are unknown.
Use a versioned URL for changed public assets; versioning and a named-provider purge have different scopes and neither clears every downstream copy.

A worker update does not replace an open document or automatically clear Cache Storage. A successful candidate normally waits for old registration clients; skipWaiting may change their controller without reloading their in-memory code. Keep old fingerprinted assets and caches until an explicit compatibility policy permits retirement.

clients.claim() is separate from skipWaiting(): an active worker may take control of eligible matching clients outside its current controlled set. Neither operation reloads a page or proves application compatibility.

For an old-asset incident, record page and worker build markers, registration states and URLs, current page controller, exact requested asset, worker cache decision, and named downstream evidence. No service-worker behavior was measured in the 28 Sep 2026 documentation-only run.
A redirect response belongs to the URI requested at that hop; every redirect in a chain is a separate cache candidate with its own Location and freshness.
301 and 308 are heuristically cacheable under RFC 9110; 302, 303, and 307 are not heuristic by default, though explicit cacheability can permit storage. No status guarantees actual reuse.
Use explicit max-age/Expires or validation when route changes need a bounded stale-target window; no-store on a new response does not delete an older redirect.
Capture status, Location, request method, cache metadata, and named-hop evidence for every response. A final URL, Age, or missing header alone does not identify the cache layer.

The Fetch Standard models user-agent HTTP-cache partitioning with top-level site as a key component; RFC 9111 matching, Vary, storage, freshness, and validation still apply, and an intermediary has its own key and policy.

Browser partitioning is not a substitute for private/no-store policy or a privacy guarantee. Chrome, Firefox, and WebKit details differ; cross-context examples in the 4 Oct 2026 documentation-only report are expected, not measured.
uncertainty: No authorized CloudFront distribution, Cloudflare zone, endpoint, controlled origin, vendor log, browser or HTTP-client capture, purge/invalidation operation, or analytics was supplied.
Actual matching rules, cache keys, POP/tier state, object residency, response rewriting, current age, and downstream copies require a live topology.
A fresh browser, direct client, one POP, one provider status, or one marker test cannot establish absence of copies or leakage everywhere.
No request may reflect history/back-forward cache or a service worker; browser DevTools controls change the experiment and do not bypass every downstream layer.
A response header, 200, 304, missing Age, missing Cache-Status, browser label, purge receipt, or invalidation completion cannot identify every producer or prove global eviction.
Cloudflare documentation describes no-cache differently in generic and OCC-specific contexts; the actual zone state and an authorized synthetic capture are needed to resolve it.
Provider-specific TTL, key, status, and purge behavior can vary by product, plan, configuration, tier, POP, and time; do not generalize either named provider.

The next useful live probe needs a fixed authorized URL, sanitized origin marker/counter, selected provider configuration, controlled request variants, named vantage, and permission to capture and if necessary purge synthetic objects.
The RFCs do not establish that a particular browser, CDN, reverse proxy, corporate proxy, service worker, or application cache implements stale extensions or applies the same precedence.

The shared s-maxage plus stale-* combination remains an implementation/configuration boundary when the strict RFC 9111 revalidation rule applies; any different named-provider result needs documentation and an authorized capture.
